question: I turn 65 on August 20, 2027, and I qualify for premium-free Part A. If I sign up for Part B in June 2027, when will my Part B coverage start?
answer: Because you're signing up before the month you turn 65, your Part B coverage starts the month you turn 65, which is August 2027. Medicare coverage always starts on the first of the month, so you'd be covered beginning August 1. June falls within your 7-month Initial Enrollment Period, which runs from 3 months before your birthday month through 3 months after it.

(an August 2027 birthday month gives a May-November 2027 window, so June is inside it). Every material claim is supported; nothing step-changing is omitted.

question: I turn 65 on July 10, 2027. I'm going to sign up for Part B in August, and I want to cancel my individual health plan so it ends the day before Part B starts. What date should I have it end?
answer: As long as you sign up within your Initial Enrollment Period, Part B coverage starts the month you turn 65. Since your birthday is in July, your Part B would begin July 1, 2027, so you could have your individual plan end on June 30. Medicare coverage always starts on the first of the month.

question: I turned 65 in March 2026 and signed up for Part B in April. My sister turned 65 in 2022, signed up late in her window, and says her coverage didn't start until two months after she enrolled. Will mine be delayed like that?
answer: No. Under 42 CFR 407.25, the delay your sister describes matches the rule for people who first became eligible before January 1, 2023: enrolling in the fifth month of the initial enrollment period started entitlement with the second month after the month of enrollment. For people first eligible on or after January 1, 2023, enrolling in any of the last 4 months of the initial enrollment period starts entitlement with the month after the month you enroll. April was the fifth month of your window (December 2025 through June 2026), so your Part B started May 1, 2026.

The sister, first eligible in 2022, falls under the pre-2023 rules.

question: I missed my Initial Enrollment Period and don't qualify for a Special Enrollment Period. I'm going to sign up for Part B on February 10, 2027, during the General Enrollment Period. When will my Part B coverage start?
answer: When you sign up during the General Enrollment Period, which runs January 1-March 31, your Part B entitlement begins on July 1 of that calendar year, so your coverage would start July 1, 2027. Because you're signing up late, you may also owe a monthly late enrollment penalty.

Correct start: March 1, 2027. Standard: the error makes coverage look later than it is (July vs March); acting on it causes no missed window, penalty, or coverage gap.

question: I turn 65 in April 2027 and I'm still working full time. I'm on my employer's group health plan, which is offered to everyone at the company, and I'll get premium-free Part A. Do I have to sign up for Part B now to avoid a penalty?
answer: No. Because your group health insurance comes from your current job and is available to everyone at the company, you can wait until you stop working (or lose that coverage, if that happens first) to sign up for Part B, and you won't pay a late enrollment penalty. Once you stop working or lose the coverage, you'll have an 8-month Special Enrollment Period to sign up. It's still worth asking your employer whether you need Part A and Part B at 65, because if you don't sign up, your job-based insurance might not cover the costs for services you get.

question: I turn 65 in June 2027 and I'm still working at a small company with 12 employees. I'm on the company's group health plan, which is offered to all employees, and I'll get premium-free Part A. Do I need to sign up for Part B?
answer: Because your employer has fewer than 20 employees, Medicare becomes your primary coverage once you're 65 and the group plan only pays after Medicare, so if you skip Part B your job-based plan may not pay for the services you get. You should plan to sign up for both Part A and Part B during your Initial Enrollment Period. It's also worth confirming with your employer's benefits administrator how the plan works with Medicare.

question: I'm 68 and never signed up for Part B because I've been covered at work. I'm retiring on January 31, 2027, but under my separation agreement my employer will keep me on its group health plan through April 30, 2027. When does my window to sign up for Part B without a penalty close?
answer: You'll have an 8-month Special Enrollment Period, and it ends 8 months after your group health plan coverage or your employment ends, whichever happens last. Since your group coverage continues through April 30, your window runs through the end of December 2027. To avoid a gap, sign up about a month before your group coverage ends.

I've elected 18 months of COBRA from my old employer and was planning to sign up for Part B when COBRA runs out. What's my window to sign up for Part B without a penalty?
answer: Because you had group health plan coverage through your job, you get an 8-month Special Enrollment Period to sign up for Part B without a late enrollment penalty. The window ends 8 months after your group health plan coverage ends. If you already have Part A, you can sign up for Part B on SSA.gov.

question: I'm a veteran turning 65 in March 2027, and I get all my health care through the VA. I'll have premium-free Part A. Can I skip Part B for now and sign up later without a penalty if I ever need it?
answer: Yes. VA health care is treated like employer coverage for Medicare purposes, so when you decide to enroll you'll qualify for a Special Enrollment Period and won't owe a late enrollment penalty. Your VA drug coverage also counts as creditable coverage, so you can hold off on a Medicare drug plan too, as long as you keep it.

question: I'm 66, still working, and contributing to an HSA through my job's high-deductible plan. I plan to retire and apply for Social Security in June 2027. When should I stop contributing to my HSA, and what happens if I don't?
answer: You and your employer should stop contributing to your HSA 6 months before you retire or apply for Social Security, so by December 2026. That's because when you apply, your premium-free Part A coverage starts 6 months back from when you sign up (but not earlier than the month you turned 65). Contributions made for months you have Medicare are subject to a 6% excise tax for every year they stay in the account.

question: I didn't sign up for Part B when I was first eligible. I had no job-based coverage and no other reason for a Special Enrollment Period. I finally signed up during this year's General Enrollment Period after waiting exactly 2 full years. What will my monthly Part B premium be for 2026?
answer: Because you waited 24 months without qualifying for a Special Enrollment Period, you'll owe a 20% late enrollment penalty: 10% for each full 12-month period you could have signed up but didn't. On the 2026 standard premium of $202.90, the penalty is $40.58, for a total of $243.48, which is rounded to $243.50 a month. You may pay more depending on your income, and the penalty is usually charged for as long as you have Part B.

question: I turn 65 in March 2027 and I'm signing up for Part A and Part B. I'm healthy, I don't take any prescriptions, and I don't have any other drug coverage. Do I need to join a drug plan now, or can I just add one later if I end up needing it?
answer: You can join a Medicare drug plan during your 7-month Initial Enrollment Period, which includes the 3 months before you turn 65, the month you turn 65, and the 3 months after. If you skip it, you can join later during the yearly Open Enrollment Period, October 15-December 7, with coverage starting January 1. You only need Part A or Part B to join a stand-alone drug plan.

question: I'm turning 65, I take no medications, and I have no other drug coverage. I'm thinking about skipping a Part D plan for my first year and joining at the next Open Enrollment Period. If I do that, how long would I be stuck paying a late enrollment penalty?
answer: Late enrollment penalties last for twice as long as you went without coverage. If you go about 12 months without creditable drug coverage, you'd owe roughly a 12% penalty, which works out to about $4.70 a month at 2026's $38.99 base premium, for 24 months. After that, your premium goes back to the plan's normal amount.

question: After my Initial Enrollment Period ended, I went 20 full months without Part D or any other creditable drug coverage. My new drug plan started January 1, 2026. How much is my monthly late enrollment penalty?
answer: Medicare calculates the penalty as 1% of the national base beneficiary premium for each full month you went without Part D or creditable coverage. The 2026 base premium is $38.99, so 20% of $38.99 is $7.798, which rounds to $7.80 a month. That amount is added to your plan's monthly premium, and you'll generally keep paying it for as long as you have Medicare drug coverage, even if you switch plans. The amount can change each year because the base premium changes.

question: I just joined a Part D plan, and it sent me a notice saying Medicare's records show a possible gap in my drug coverage, along with a form asking about my prior coverage. I had drug coverage through my former employer's retiree plan that I believe was creditable. How long do I have to send the form back?
answer: You have 30 days from the date on the notice to complete, sign, and return the form. This is your chance to tell the plan about creditable coverage it didn't know about, so include your retiree drug coverage details; if you don't, you may be charged a late enrollment penalty. You can also call your plan to let them know you had prior creditable coverage.

question: I'm 67 and already have Part A and Part B. I've had creditable drug coverage through my employer, and it ends when I retire on December 31, 2026. How long do I have to join a Medicare drug plan?
answer: Leaving employer coverage gives you a Special Enrollment Period to join a Medicare drug plan or a Medicare Advantage Plan. Your chance to join lasts for 3 full months after the month your coverage ends, so you have through March 31, 2027. To avoid the Part D late enrollment penalty, don't go 63 or more days in a row without creditable drug coverage, so it's best to have your new plan start January 1.

question: I'm in a Medicare Advantage plan in Ohio and I'm moving to Arizona on June 15, which is outside my plan's service area. I plan to tell my plan about the move in May. When can I switch plans, and what are my options?
answer: Because you're telling your plan before you move, your chance to switch begins the month before the month you move, which is May, and continues for 2 full months after you move. During that time you can switch to a new Medicare Advantage Plan (with or without drug coverage) or a Medicare drug plan, or go back to Original Medicare. If you don't join a new Medicare Advantage Plan during this Special Enrollment Period, you'll be enrolled in Original Medicare when you're dropped from your old plan.

question: I've been in a Medicare Advantage plan since 2025. It's February 2027, and I want to drop it, go back to Original Medicare, and pick up a stand-alone drug plan. Can I do that now?
answer: Yes. If you're already in a Medicare Advantage Plan, the Medicare Advantage Open Enrollment Period runs January 1-March 31, and during it you can drop your plan and go back to Original Medicare; if you do, you'll be able to join a Medicare drug plan. You can only make one change each year during this period, and changes take effect the first day of the month after the plan gets your request.

question: I'm 52 and started getting Social Security disability benefits in January 2025. I'd like to wait as long as I can. When can I join a Medicare drug plan?
answer: If you're getting Social Security disability benefits, you'll get Medicare automatically after 24 months of benefits. Your chance to join a Medicare Advantage Plan or a Medicare drug plan starts 21 months after you start getting disability benefits. If you ask to join before your Medicare Part A and/or Part B starts, your plan coverage starts the same day your Medicare does.

question: My mother is moving to a skilled nursing facility after a hospital stay, and her doctors expect her to need about 30 days there in 2026. She has Original Medicare. What will she owe for the stay under Part A?

question: My father has Original Medicare and has never used any lifetime reserve days. His doctors expect a single hospital stay of about 160 days in 2026. What will he pay under Part A?
answer: In 2026, he'd pay the $1,736 deductible for the benefit period, then $0 for the first 60 days. For days 61-90 he'd pay $434 per day, and after day 90 he'd pay $868 for each lifetime reserve day he uses.

question: I retired in 2025. My 2024 income was $180,000 filing as an individual, but this year my income is only about $60,000. Am I stuck paying a higher Part B premium in 2026?
answer: Your 2026 Part B premium is based on the modified adjusted gross income on your tax return from 2 years ago, so with $180,000 in 2024 income as an individual filer you'd pay $527.50 a month. However, retirement counts as a life-changing event, so you can ask Social Security to use your current, lower income by filing Form SSA-44. If they approve it, you'd pay the standard $202.90 premium.
